newsitem.title: UK: Pro-Europe Labour says joining EMU hangs on jobs.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Europe Labour says joining EMU hangs on jobs.

text.p: The opposition Labour Party, mocking the "narrow nationalism" of the ruling Conservatives, vowed on Tuesday to make Britain a leading player in Europe if it wins the forthcoming election.

But in a speech to the party's last pre-election conference, foreign affairs spokesman Robin Cook reaffirmed that a Labour government would sign up for the European Union's planned single currency only if it helped to tackle unemployment.
"Jobs will be the bottom line by which we judge whether Britain will join any single currency," Cook told delegates.

He said Labour, out of power since 1979, supported a drive by the Scandinavian members of the EU to add objectives to reduce unemployment to the financial and economic criteria that will underpin economic and monetary union (EMU).
"The single market would work better with a single currency. But Britain will only benefit if we can compete on level terms.

"That is why Labour believes that, for Britain to join a single currency, we need first to achieve convergence of economic performance in the real world of output, of investment and of jobs," Cook told the conference, the last before Britain's general election, which must be held by May.
Labour, like the Conservatives, is determined to keep its options open on membership of EMU for as long as possible.

But in a clear difference between the parties, Cook said Labour would back a European directive limiting the working week for most employees to 48 hours and would sign up for the EU's social chapter on workers' rights by the end of 1998.

"We will do it because Britain cannot be a leading player in Europe when it is lagging behind everyone else in Europe," he said. The Conservatives say the social chapter would destroy jobs by adding burdens to business.

Enlargement of the EU would be a Labour priority, and Cook announced the appointment of Sir Michael Butler, a former British ambassador to the EU, as a special envoy to the dozen countries that have applied for membership.

Cook taunted the Conservatives for their deep divisions over Europe and said the threat to Britain was that the ruling party's civil war was being won by those whose real agenda was to withdraw from Europe.
"Britain cannot face the challenge of the modern world through the tunnel vision of the narrow nationalism of today's Tory party," Cook said.
The Conservatives' "crude jingoism" was damaging not only relations with the rest of Europe but also British society.

"Once a nation is persuaded that foreigners abroad are a threat, then it is only a short stop to believing that minorities at home are a danger. Xenophobia and jingoism are the natural parents of bigotry and discrimination," he said.
